full_judgment: 10. Having accepted such power of the High Court Division to make a Judicial Interference with any judgment, order or sentence of the Appellate Tribunal Constituted under the Special Powers act, the question now arises as to what is the exact nature and limitation of such jurisdiction by way of a judicial interference by the High Court Division under its supervisory and superintending authority over Courts sub-ordinate thereto under Article 109 of the Constitution. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 where the High Courts were vested with the powers of superintendence over all Courts and Tribunals throughout the territory in relation to which the High Court's concerned exercised its jurisdiction. The main distinction between the provision of Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and the erstwhile Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment 1976 is that whereas under Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh the supervisory and superintending authority of the High Court Division extend to the Courts sub-ordinate thereto, whereas under erstwhile 227(1) of the Indian Constitution prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 the superintending jurisdiction of the High Courts extended over all Courts and Tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction irrespective of the fact whether such Courts and Tribunals were sub-ordinate to the High Courts concerned. This difference between the two provisions in the Bangladesh and Indian Constitutions as before has been further narrowed down in view of the fact that Bangladesh Constitution as per Article 114 thereof does not contemplate the establishment of any Court of law including any judicial tribunal exercising the function of a court of law which is not otherwise sub-ordinate to the Supreme Court. Erstwhile Article 227(1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976 came up for consideration before the various High Courts and Supreme Court in India to determine its scope and authority with relation to the power of the High Courts to make judicial interference with any judgment or order of any other court as such. The extent and scope of the judicial superintendence of the High Court over other courts came for consideration in various High Courts and Supreme Courts in India and the consensus view on such question appears to be that where there is a patent absence or excess erroneous assumption of jurisdiction and grave error of law apparent on the face of the record, such power of the High Court is to be exercised most sparingly in appropriate cases only in order to keep the courts concerned within the limits of their authority under the law. The power of judicial superintendence of the High Courts over the Courts below by its nature is a revisional one short of an appeal; it is not intended to correct any and every mistake of law but only such grave error of law which causes miscarriage of justice as such. Taking into consideration the views of the Indian Supreme Court from time to time with regard to the power of the High Court to make judicial interference with any judgment and order of the Courts below under erstwhile Article 227 (1) of the Constitution of India prior to 42nd amendment of 1976, it can safely be said that Article 109 of the Constitution of Bangladesh has conferred upon the High Court Division of the Supreme Court such superintending authority over the courts below where under the High Court Division can make judicial interference with any judgment and order of any other Court of law including a judicial tribunal exercising the functions of a court of law, such as the Appellate Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, by way of a revision short of an appeal to rectify any patent absence or excess or erroneous assumption of jurisdiction, or any grave error of Jaw apparent on the face of the record which might cause serious miscarriage of justice. The High Court Division in exercising such jurisdiction as contemplated under Article 109 of the Constitution may refer to the inherent residuary revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division short of its appellate powers under the normal procedural law, and even without such reference can also directly resort to the jurisdiction conferred upon it under Article 109 of the Constitution, as a distinct forum for a separate proceeding thereunder, being quite separate, distinct and independent from the extraordinary prerogative jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.
